bullets: How light and sound travel as waves, and how to use the wave equation
slides.heading: Waves: light, sound and the wave equation
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we are going to compare light and sound as waves, use the wave equation, and by the end you will be able to explain exactly why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

bullets: Tell transverse light waves apart from longitudinal sound waves
Use v = f x wavelength to find a wave speed, a frequency or a wavelength
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these two things.

bullets: On a storm night you see a lightning flash, then hear the thunder seconds later
Why does the flash arrive first - and what does the gap tell us about the two waves?
slides.heading: First the flash, then the thunder
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands and take two or three guesses without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because the speeds of light and sound are the key to the whole lesson.

bullets: Light is a transverse wave: the vibration is across the direction of travel
Sound is a longitudinal wave: the particles bunch and spread along the direction of travel
Every wave carries energy while its particles only vibrate in place
slides.heading: Two kinds of wave, one shared idea
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: the kind of wave is set by how the particles vibrate compared with the direction the energy travels.

bullets: Light is transverse: the dot bobs up and down as the wave races to the right
Sound is longitudinal: the particles bunch and spread while the energy moves on
slides.heading: Light and sound are different kinds of waves
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the dot on the light wave bob up and down in place, then watch the sound particles bunch and spread - neither particle travels with the wave.

bullets: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: v = f x wavelength
For sound in air, 340 m/s = 170 Hz x 2 m
slides.heading: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength
slides.notes: Tell them to watch one full wave under the bracket: that length is the wavelength, and multiplying it by how many waves pass each second gives the speed.

bullets: Tempting wrong turn: Sound travels faster than light.
Light is far faster: the lightning flash arrives first and the thunder follows
slides.heading: A common mistake: we see lightning before we hear thunder
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: the thunder feels powerful, but the flash reaches you almost instantly while the sound crawls in at 340 metres per second.

bullets: Waves carry energy while the particles only vibrate in place
Speed, frequency and wavelength always obey v = f x wavelength, and light leaves sound far behind
slides.heading: What the wave examples have in common
slides.notes: Pull the threads together: whatever the kind of wave, the energy is what travels, the particles stay put, and the wave equation ties speed, frequency and wavelength together.

bullets: Step 1: rearrange the wave equation, wavelength = v / f
Step 2: wavelength = 340 / 170 = 2 m, and check 170 Hz x 2 m = 340 m/s
slides.heading: Worked example: finding a wavelength
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: notice the check multiplies frequency by wavelength and lands back on the speed we started with.

bullets: Work out the wavelength of a sound wave with v = 340 m/s and f = 170 Hz: rearrange first, then calculate
Careful - a classmate writes Sound travels faster than light. Explain to them why that is wrong, using lightning and thunder
slides.heading: Your turn: calculate, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs two minutes, then cold-call one pair and press them on the trap: if sound really were faster, which would you notice first in a storm, the flash or the thunder?

bullets: Calculate a wavelength from a speed and a frequency, showing the rearrangement
Explain why this claim is wrong: Sound travels faster than light.
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the words light is far faster in your last answer - if you can explain why the flash arrives before the thunder, you have cracked today's lesson.
